title: You Can’t System Your Way Out of the Wrong People
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder argues that process cannot compensate for personnel: clean SOPs, a good tech stack and a well-architected execution model all fail in the hands of people who are misaligned, unaccountable or not capable. The piece is built out of her own hiring confessions — keeping people too long because she liked them or felt bad, hiring on recommendation without asking for proof of performance, retaining people who were good at something other than what the business needed, and repeatedly lowering the bar. Her claim about the cost is specific and cultural rather than merely operational: a B player does not just reduce output, they teach the rest of the team that the stated standard is not real. She names the trap as loyalty without clarity, which she calls martyrdom, and points out the misalignment between saying you want a $10M or $100M company and tolerating someone who clearly is not cutting it. The practical instrument she lands on is a retrospective hiring test — would I hire this person today, knowing what I now know — followed by the cost question if the answer is no. The closing line does the argumentative work: the people are the system, so the system cannot be fixed around them.
points: The reframe worth keeping: tolerating a misaligned hire is a public statement to the team that your standards are negotiable.
Mulder identifies the real reasons underperformers get kept — affection, guilt, effort mistaken for fit, and hiring fatigue — rather than any business rationale.
Her 'would I hire this person today?' test converts a vague discomfort into a decision, with the follow-up cost question forcing action.
She distinguishes being good at something from being good at the thing the business currently needs, which is where most retention mistakes hide.
The cost of the wrong person is counted in four currencies here: money, morale, momentum and the leader's own energy.
quotes: I’m going to say something I wish someone had forced me to hear sooner: It’s not just about the systems. It’s about who’s running them.

You can have the cleanest SOPs, the smartest tech stack, the most well-architected execution model, but if the people executing it aren’t aligned, accountable, or capable… it breaks. Or worse, it drains you while slowly killing the vision.
Over the years, I’ve held onto people way too long. And it wasn’t because they were the right fit. Usually it was because I liked them.
I’ve kept people who were good at something, just not the thing we actually needed. I’ve made excuses, told myself I was being too harsh, and lowered the bar more than once.

Hiring a B player doesn’t just hurt output; it breaks culture. Keeping someone misaligned teaches the rest of the team that your standards aren’t real. Your systems are only as strong as the people upholding them.
But loyalty without clarity becomes martyrdom. And you weren’t put on this planet to die on the hill of someone else’s unfulfilled potential.
The right people make the systems sing. The wrong people make the systems feel like more work.
